extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general literate public interested in moral and satirical essays (early-18th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for composing satirical and moral essays: selecting proper targets for satire, rhetorical tactics (use of classical examples), and a moral framework for judging actions by intention and category (good/evil/indifferent).

rubrics_metrics.name: satire_target_selection
rubrics_metrics.description: A Satyr should expose nothing but what is corrigible, and make a due Discrimination between those who are, and those who are not the proper Objects of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not level invective at an entire sex or species; avoid 'levelling Satyrs' that censure the whole species (these are of no use to the world). Satire ought to point at vices or frailties that can be corrected; make distinctions between proper and improper objects of satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_universal_censure
rubrics_metrics.description: Such levelling Satyrs are of no Use to the World, and for this Reason I have often wondered how the French Author... could think human Nature a proper Subject for Satyr.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism that paints a whole class or the entire human species as wholly vicious fails to correct vice and undermines the purpose of satiric writing; aim for particular, correctible targets rather than sweeping denunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_classical_examples_in_moral_essays
rubrics_metrics.description: When I employ myself upon a Paper of Morality, I generally consider how I may recommend the particular Virtue which I treat of, by the Precepts or Examples of the ancient Heathens; by that Means, if possible, to shame those who have greater Advantages of knowing their Duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy precepts and examples from classical (pagan) authorities to shame or persuade readers—especially effective to rebuke those who should know better. Using admired ancient examples lends weight and cross-confessional appeal to moral argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: divide_actions_and_evaluate_by_intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Cast all our Actions under the Division of such as are in themselves either Good, Evil, or Indifferent. A good Intention joined to a good Action, gives it its proper Force and Efficacy; joined to an Evil Action, extenuates its Malignity, and in some Cases may take it wholly away; and joined to an indifferent Action turns it to a Virtue, and makes it meritorious as far as human Actions can be so. An Evil Intention perverts the best of Actions, and makes them... shining Sins. An indifferent Intention destroys the Merit of a good Action; abates, but never takes away, the Malignity of an evil Action; and leaves an indifferent Action in its natural State of Indifference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral actions (or when arguing morally), classify acts as good/evil/indifferent and attend to the actor's intention—intentions materially change moral value. Use this schema to explain how the same external act can vary in moral worth depending on inner purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: habitual_good_intention_as_moral_standard
rubrics_metrics.description: It is therefore of unspeakable Advantage to possess our Minds with an habitual good Intention, and to aim all our Thoughts, Words, and Actions at some laudable End... This is a sort of Thrift or Good-Husbandry in moral Life, which does not throw away any single Action, but makes every one go as far as it can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate cultivating a continual disposition of good intention so that even indifferent actions become meritorious; present this habitual intention as both a theological/moral ideal and a practical method to make ordinary life count toward virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: beware_elevating_indifferent_actions_into_duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Injunction of superfluous Ceremonies makes such Actions Duties, as were before indifferent... renders Religion more burdensome and difficult... betrays many into Sins of Omission... and fixes the Minds of the Vulgar to the shadowy unessential Points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique religious or social practices that convert indifferent acts into binding duties: doing so distracts from essential moral matters and imposes needless burdens. When composing moral critique, argue against conflating externals/ceremonies with true virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: rhetorical_authority_example_socrates
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce instances like the Speech of Socrates: 'Whether or no God will approve of my Actions, I know not; but this I am sure of, that I have at all Times made it my Endeavour to please him...'—use such examples to exemplify the habitual good intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use admired historical/philosophical exemplars (Socrates, Erasmus's praise) as rhetorical authority to illustrate and ennoble the virtue you recommend; such exemplars can make a persuasive emotional and intellectual appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: strategies_for_dealing_with_patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: There are but two Ways of doing any thing with great People, and those are by making your self either considerable or agreeable: The former is not to be attained but by finding a Way to live without them, or concealing that you want them; the latter is only by falling into their Taste and Pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As practical social advice (relevant to clients, dependants, or writers seeking patronage): either cultivate independent worth/necessity (be 'considerable') or adapt to patrons' tastes and pleasures (be 'agreeable'), noting the moral and psychological costs of forced agreeableness (imitation of faults, subservience).
